tests.title: Turret follows the goal with the camera

why.p: A turret that follows the goal takes the aiming off the drivers. It must turn the short way, never go past its limits, and say clearly when the goal is out of range. Every turret is built differently (gear ratio, range, where the camera is), so we need other turrets.

ul: Hard stops on the turret just past `min` and `max`. Check them by hand first.
Cables slack over the whole range. The flywheel off (do not fire in this test).
Safety glasses if the launcher has pieces in it.
`Turret.motor(...).gearRatio(...).follows(camera)` in `Robot.java`, `Tunables.Turret` with `min`, `max`.
A goal tag (AprilTag) you can see: the field, or a printed tag at the right height.

The turret at its `startAngle` before INIT (by default 0 = straight forward; a mark or a jig helps), unless it has a home switch ([TUR-01](repo:testing/tests/TUR-01.md)) or an absolute encoder. TeleOp started within 5 minutes of another program starts from the angle that program ended at.
Simulator: lesson 9's turret robot (`turretbot`) commands, then "TurretBot TeleOp".

ol: INIT your TeleOp, START. Drive (or turn the robot) until the camera sees the goal.
Watch the turret turn to the goal. Read the turret line on the Driver Station.
Turn the robot slowly 90 degrees one way, then the other. The turret keeps on the goal.
Turn the robot until the goal is past a turret limit: the turret waits at the limit, and the Driver Station says "goal out of turret range".
Gamepad 2 right stick X: the turret turns by hand. Let go: following goes on.
Gamepad 2 BACK: following off. BACK again: on.

pass.p: In steps 2 and 3 the turret stays within its `tolerance` (1.5 degrees by default) of the goal while the robot turns slowly, it never goes past `min` or `max` (0 times), and step 4 shows the message.

ul: camera (Limelight or webcam), on the turret or on the body
gear ratio, `min`, `max`, `kP` you used
how far off it settled (degrees, from the Driver Station or by eye)
any shaking or overshoot, and when

different.p: A camera on the robot's body needs `.cameraOnBody()`: say if you used it. A turret with a different range (say 0 to 270), a servo turret ([TUR-03](repo:testing/tests/TUR-03.md)) or a slip ring ([TUR-04](repo:testing/tests/TUR-04.md)) is very useful. If the turret turns away from the goal, `.reversed()` fixes it: say whether the docs made that clear.

tests.title: Odometry backup aim when the camera is covered

why.p: When a tag is hidden, the turret should keep aiming from the odometry. A wrong goal point, a wrong alliance or a pose that was never set would aim at the wrong place, so the library has checks. We need to see them work on other robots.

ul: As AIM-01: hard stops, slack cables, flywheel off.
AIM-01 passed. ODO-01 passed.
`Tunables.Aim`: `goalX`, `goalY` (inches, seen from your own drivers' wall; BIOBUZZ: `goalX = 13, goalY = -13`, your HIVE's CELL that is up at the start), and for BIOBUZZ `mirrorForRed = false`.
An autonomous that ends near the goal, or the "set pose here" spot (ODO-02).

ol: Run your autonomous (or set the pose with START held 1 s), then INIT TeleOp. Read INIT's `Aim:` line (alliance, goal, mirrorForRed).
START. Point the turret at the goal with the camera seeing it (`following: camera`).
Cover the camera with your hand. The turret keeps pointing at the goal, and the Driver Station says `following: odometry`.
With the camera still covered, drive about 3 ft sideways. The turret follows the goal.
Uncover the camera. Read any `Aim: camera says ... odometry ...` warning.
Run TeleOp with no autonomous and no pose set: it must say `Aim odometry: the pose was never set`, and covering the camera must stop following.

pass.p: With the camera covered, the turret points within 5 degrees of the goal (by eye or by the Driver Station) after the 3 ft drive, and in step 6 it does not follow from the odometry (0 times).

ul: odometry kind, camera kind
`goalX`, `goalY` you used
how far off the odometry aim was after step 4 (degrees)
the camera/odometry disagreement it showed in step 5 (inches), if any

different.p: Use your own goal point if you test on a different field or a practice goal. If your turret robot has no camera (only odometry), use `.followsOdometry()` and skip step 3; say so. On RED, check that the `Aim:` line matches the field.

tests.title: Whole-robot aim - the robot turns to the goal while you drive

why.p: Most robots have no turret: they aim by turning. Whole-robot aim turns the robot to the goal while the driver drives, and the turn stick always wins. Drive trains turn very differently, so the numbers (`turnKp`, `minTurnPower`) need testing on many robots.

ul: Clear floor, PRACTICE profile. The robot turns by itself while aim is on.
Hand near STOP, and the driver ready to let go of the button.
A camera with `.goal(...)`, or odometry with `Tunables.Aim.goalX`, `goalY`.
In `Controls.java`: `g1.rb.toggle(robot.aimMode()).says("aim the robot at the goal on/off").rumble();`
Simulator: lesson 9's `flywheelbot` commands, then "FlywheelBot TeleOp".

ol: INIT your TeleOp, START. Drive until the goal is in view (or the pose is set, with odometry).
Turn the robot about 45 degrees away from the goal. Press RB: the robot turns to face the goal.
With aim on, drive forward and sideways (mecanum) or forward only (tank). The robot keeps facing the goal.
Push the turn stick: the robot turns as the stick says. Let go: the aim takes over again.
Hide the goal (cover the camera, no odometry): it must not turn by itself (`Aim: no goal`).
Press RB again: aim off.

pass.p: In step 2 the robot ends within `toleranceDeg` (2 degrees by default) of the goal within 2 seconds, and in step 5 it does not turn by itself (0 degrees).

ul: drive type, camera or odometry
`turnKp`, `maxTurnPower`, `minTurnPower` you ended with
how far off it stopped (degrees) and how long it took (seconds)
any shaking, and when

different.p: A tank drive can only drive forward while it aims: that is expected. If it stops a few degrees short, try `minTurnPower` and say what worked. If you put aim on another button, say which. A robot with a turret that follows the goal must NOT use this (INIT stops): that message is worth reporting if it was unclear.

tests.title: Pause at BACK, and START-then-BACK pairs

why.p: BACK is the panic button: it must pause the robot at the press, even if the driver holds it. START and BACK together (START first) are the debug lines. If BACK goes down first, it must stay a plain pause and never start the robot again by itself.

ul: Real robot: low power, clear floor. You will stop the robot while it moves.
Any robot in five files with its TeleOp. Simulator: any robot (a kit bot from SIM-01 is fine). In the simulator, BACK is the Backspace key and START is Enter.

ol: INIT, START. Drive forward and run a mechanism (an intake).
Press BACK: everything stops at once, the Driver Station says PAUSED. Keep holding BACK for 3 s: the robot stays stopped.
Let go, then tap BACK: everything goes on (the intake runs again).
On gamepad 1, hold the small START button, then press BACK. Let go of both: the debug lines show. The robot does not pause.
Press BACK first, then START: it is a plain pause. Let go of both: the robot stays paused. Tap BACK to go on.
Hold BACK for 1 s with field-centric on: it pauses and resets "forward". Robot-centric: a note says "forward" is only reset in field-centric.

pass.p: The robot stops within 0.2 s of the BACK press in steps 2 and 5, never starts again while BACK is held or after BACK-then-START (0 times), and step 4 shows the debug lines without a pause.

ul: robot, one driver or two
how fast it stopped (about)
what step 4 and step 5 did
anything that surprised the driver

different.p: If you moved pause or debug to other buttons (`libraryButtons`), use yours and say which. A Logitech or PS controller names the buttons differently (Share, Options): say which controller you used.

tests.title: Quick start from a blank robot project

why.p: The Quick start promises a driving robot in 30 minutes. A student who has never used the library should be able to follow it alone. Every place you get stuck is a docs fix for us.

ul: Real robot: on a block for the first drive (the Quick start says when), low power.
A robot project in Android Studio that builds (the FTC SDK's FtcRobotController), with no ftc-helper-lib yet.
Best: a student who has not used the library before does it, and a second person writes notes without helping.
A timer.

ol: Start the timer. Follow the [Quick start](repo:docs/quick-start.md) from the top, exactly as written.
Each time you are stuck for more than 2 minutes, write the step and the words that confused you.
Real robot: build, install, run the Hardware Check, drive. Simulator: the Quick start's simulator part.
Stop the timer when the robot drives (or the simulator robot drives).

pass.p: The robot drives within 60 minutes, with no help from someone who knows the library (0 times asked).

ul: time to a driving robot (minutes)
each place you got stuck (step and words), and what got you going again
Windows, Mac, Linux or Chromebook; real robot or simulator
which way you got the five files (from the configuration, a template, a kit bot)

different.p: Any robot that drives is fine; a kit bot can use [Pick your template](repo:docs/templates.md). The simulator alone also counts (no robot): say so. A student with no Java at all is the most useful tester.

tests.title: First drive with the five files - wheels, sticks, slow and pause

why.p: Driving is the first thing a team sees work. We want to know that the drive line in `Robot.java` works on many drivetrains, and that the motor-direction steps in lesson 2 find a wrong wheel.

ul: First run with the robot on a block, wheels off the ground.
Keep `maxPower` and `practiceMaxPower` at 0.4 in `Tunables.java` for this test.
A clear floor and a hand near the Driver Station STOP button.
The robot in five files with your drive line (from the Quick start or a template).
Your TeleOp built and installed.

ol: Robot on a block. INIT your TeleOp, then START.
Push the left stick up. Every wheel must roll the way that moves the robot forward. Fix any wheel with lesson 2 section 7, and count how many fixes you needed.
Put the robot on the floor. Left stick up for about 2 seconds: it drives straight.
Right stick right: it turns clockwise. Mecanum only: left stick right strafes right.
Pull LT all the way while driving: the robot goes slower. (One driver, `oneDriver = true`: click the left stick for slow on and off.)
Press BACK on gamepad 1: the robot stops the moment the button goes down, and the Driver Station says PAUSED. Let go, then tap BACK again: it drives again.
Tap GUIDE: the button map shows. Tap GUIDE again to close it.

pass.p: The robot drives straight within about 6 in of drift over 5 ft, turns the right way, LT slows it, and BACK stops it within 0.5 s of the press.

ul: drive type and motors (for example "mecanum, 4 x goBILDA 312")
how many wheels needed a direction fix, and which steps you used
drift over 5 ft (inches, left or right)
how fast BACK stopped the robot (about)

different.p: Any drivetrain the library can drive is in scope: 2-motor or 4-motor tank, mecanum, a kit bot's drive. If your robot has a drivetrain the library does not offer (swerve, H-drive), report that as "could not run" and say what it is. If your driver uses other buttons (`libraryButtons` in `Controls.java`), use those and say which.

tests.title: Hood Finder on a servo hood - stops and angles

why.p: The hood's two stops (`posA`, `posB`) are hard limits: the hood never goes past them. The Hood Finder finds them without code. A servo pushing on a stop gets hot and breaks, so this must be clear and safe on hoods built differently from ours.

ul: Flywheel off. Fingers away from the hood while it moves.
Listen for a humming servo: back off at once.
`.hood(Hood.servo("hood"))` on the launcher in `Robot.java` (no `Tunables.Hood` numbers needed yet).
The Hood Finder OpMode ([recipe](repo:docs/cookbook.md#how-do-i-find-my-hoods-stops-and-angles)).
A phone angle app (optional, for angles).

ol: Start the Hood Finder. Choose a START POINT near where the hood sits (D-pad; nothing moves), press A.
Nudge toward one stop (D-pad right/left 0.01, up/down 0.05, hold RB for finer). Stop when it JUST touches, back off a hair, press X.
Do the same at the other stop, press B. The screen shows `Tunables.Hood: posA = ..., posB = ...`.
Optional: lay the phone on the hood at each stop and type the angle (hold LB + D-pad) before X or B.
Copy the line(s) into `Tunables.java`. Time a stop-to-stop move for `travelSec`.
In your TeleOp: START sends the hood to `startAngle` (in `Tunables.Hood`). Gamepad 2 left stick moves it: push it hard both ways.

pass.p: In step 6 the hood never touches a stop (0 hums or stalls in 10 pushes each way), and it stays between `posA` and `posB`.

ul: hood design (servo, gears or linkage, range in degrees)
the `Tunables.Hood` line it printed
`travelSec` you measured
anything that hummed, and when

different.p: A linkage (equal servo steps do not make equal angles): add points in between with A to get a `calibration` line. A hood that goes the other way round is fine: say so. A CR-servo hood is not supported yet: report "could not run" and what you have.

tests.title: Motor hood - stops by hand, and it arrives before firing

why.p: A motor hood knows where it is (its encoder), so the launcher waits until it arrives. Its ticks count from where it is at INIT, so the start position matters. We have not tested a motor hood on a robot yet.

ul: Flywheel off for steps 1-4. Low `maxPower` (0.3) at first. Fingers away from the hood.
Hard stops on the hood at both ends.
`.hood(Hood.motor("hood", "motor-id"))` on the launcher.
The Hood Finder OpMode.

ol: Put the hood on the stop you want as 0 ticks (stop A). Start the Hood Finder: nothing is powered.
Move the hood by hand to near stop A (a hair off), press X. To near stop B, press B.
Copy `posA`, `posB` (ticks) into `Tunables.Hood`. Set `maxPower = 0.3`.
In your TeleOp (hood on stop A at INIT): START. Move the hood with gamepad 2 left stick to each end. It must stop before each stop.
With a shot table that has a hood column, spin up and fire one at two distances: the launcher waits for `hood` until the hood arrives (`Launcher waits for: hood`).

pass.p: The hood stops within 2% of its range before each stop (never stalls on a stop), and in step 5 no piece is fed while the hood is more than `tolerance` away (0 of 2).

ul: hood motor, gearing, range in ticks
the `posA`, `posB` you got, and `kP`, `maxPower`, `tolerance` you used
how long the hood took to arrive in step 5 (seconds)
what happened if the hood was NOT on stop A at INIT (try it once, carefully, at low power)

different.p: A hood that is not near a stop at INIT will count from the wrong place: that is how it is built today. If your robot cannot start on a stop, tell us why: we may add homing.

tests.title: Interlock rule - two parts are never in their zones at once

why.p: An interlock rule (`keepApart(...)` in `Robot.java`) keeps two parts that share space from crashing, whoever moves them: a button, a stick, an action, a turret that follows the goal. If it lets both in once, two parts can break. We test it on our turret and wrist; your two parts are different.

ul: Simulator first. On the real robot, start with slow powers (`maxPower` 0.3 for both parts).
Measure the zones by moving the parts by hand, with the power off. Never let the test be the first time the two parts come near each other.
A hand on STOP. Hard stops still on the robot: the rule does not replace them.
Two parts with a position (a turret, lift, arm, wrist, claw, positioner or hood) that can hit each other.

One line in `Robot.java` after the parts, for example `keepApart("TurretLift", turret.zone(), lift.zoneAbove());`, and its section in `Tunables.java` with your measured zones (`turretFrom`, `turretTo`, `liftAbove`), as in the [interlocks guide](repo:docs/guides/interlocks.md#the-idea-with-a-turret-and-a-lift).

Simulator (no robot of your own yet): the V2 example robot. In the `ftc-helper-lib` folder: `./gradlew :sim:fromRobot -PteamCode=none -ProbotClass=com.crossbotics.ftchelper.examples.v2bot.Robot -Pout=build/v2bot.properties`, then `./gradlew :sim:run -PteamCode=none -Probot=build/v2bot.properties`, open http://localhost:8780 and choose "V2 Bot TeleOp". Its rule is `TurretClaw`: turret 147 to 217 degrees, wrist 0 to 47 degrees.

ol: INIT. Read the `Interlock ...` line: it names both parts and both zones, in each part's units (degrees, counts, servo position).
START. Put part A in its zone (V2: the wrist folded, as it starts).

Move part B toward its zone with its stick or button (V2: gamepad 2 right stick X turns the turret toward the back). Part B stops before its zone, and the Driver Station shows one line, for example `TurretClaw : Turret held at ... deg: Wrist is between ...`.
Keep asking part B to go in for 5 s. It stays out.

Move part A out of its zone (V2: gamepad 2 Y, score in a FLOWER: the wrist swings out). Part B now goes in: by itself if a button sent it to a target (the target is kept), or while you still push its stick.
Now B is in its zone. Ask A to go back in (V2: gamepad 2 X, stow). A waits outside its zone until B leaves.
Run an action or an autonomous step that moves both parts at once. Read which one waits.
Put a wrong number in the rule's Tunables section (say `liftAbove` larger than the lift's `max`). INIT must stop and say what is wrong. Put it back.

pass.p: The two parts are never both in their zones (0 times in steps 3 to 7), the waiting part goes on by itself once the other leaves (2 of 2, steps 5 and 6), and step 8 stops INIT with a message that names the rule.

ul: your two parts (kinds, motor or servo) and the zones you wrote, in their units
how far outside its zone each waiting part stopped (degrees, counts or position)
the Driver Station line while it held a part (copy it)
the INIT message from step 8
simulator or real robot

different.p: Any two parts with a position work: an arm and an intake that folds out, a wrist and a low lift, a hood and a turret. A part with no position (an intake roller) needs `Zone.when(...)` with your own sensor: say if you used it. If your parts can only hit at some lift heights, a rule with a narrower zone may be enough: say what you chose and why.

tests.title: Interlock stop distance - a fast part brakes before its zone

why.p: A motor does not stop the moment it is told to: the robot only decides once per loop, and a braking motor still coasts. The rule works out each part's stop distance from its speed and the slowest recent loops, and slows it down in time. We tested it in the simulator (a turret at about 680 degrees a second); real lifts and turrets are heavier and slower to stop.

ul: ILK-01 passed first, on this robot, with slow powers.
Real robot: raise the power in steps (0.3, 0.6, then full). Stop at once if a part ends inside its zone.
Fingers away from both parts. A hand on STOP.
An interlock rule that works at low power (ILK-01).
The part that moves fast toward its zone (usually the turret or the lift) at its normal `maxPower`.
Simulator: the V2 example robot as in ILK-01 (its turret is fast).
Optional: `<part>StopSec` in the rule's Tunables section (for example `turretStopSec = 0.15`, the default).

ol: INIT, START. Put the other part in its zone (V2: wrist folded).
Push the fast part's stick fully toward its zone and hold it. Watch where it stops. Read its angle or counts on the Driver Station.
Write how far outside its zone it stopped. It should slow down near its waiting point, then stop there (two margins outside the zone).
Do it 5 times, from different starting places (near the zone and far from it).
Make the loops slow on purpose: turn on a camera, or run the simulator with other programs busy. Repeat step 2 three times.
If it ever ended inside the zone, or past its waiting point: raise `<part>StopSec` (say 0.25), INIT again, and repeat.

pass.p: In all 8 tries (steps 4 and 5) the part stops outside its zone (0 times inside), within about one margin of its waiting point.

ul: the fast part, its motor and gear ratio, its `maxPower`
the zone edge, its waiting point, and where it stopped each time
the `StopSec` you ended with (and the margin, if you set one)
simulator or real robot; slow loops: how you made them

different.p: A servo part needs no stop distance (it is never sent past its fence): test a motor part. A lift that moves fast downward with gravity is a good test: say which way it moved. If your part has no motor id in `Robot.java` (`.part(...)` or a motor id), the rule learns its top speed from the fastest it has seen: say if the first runs stopped later than the later ones.

tests.title: A lift or arm on two motors - same power, same moment

why.p: Many lifts have a motor on each side. If the two motors get different powers, or one turns the wrong way, they fight: they get hot and can break a gearbox or bend the slide. `alsoMotor` and `alsoMotorReversed` send every power to both motors in the same loop. We tested it in the simulator and with the test kit; real two-motor lifts are needed.

ul: **Chain or belt OFF for steps 1 and 2.** Two motors that fight can break a gearbox.
Low power first (`maxPower` 0.3 in the lift's Tunables section). Fingers out of the slide.
A hand on STOP. Hard stops at both ends.

The lift's line in `Robot.java` with its second motor: `lift = add(Lift.slide("lift_left").alsoMotorReversed("lift_right"));` (or `alsoMotor` when both turn the same way). An arm: `Arm.motor(...).alsoMotorReversed(...)`.
The encoder cable in the FIRST motor (`lift_left`). The Tunables section is the first motor's name in CamelCase (`Tunables.LiftLeft`).

ol: Chain or belt off. INIT: read `LiftLeft: two motors, "lift_left" (its encoder is read) and "lift_right" (...)`.
START. Push the lift's stick up a little. Both motor shafts must turn the way that lifts. One wrong? Use the other method (`alsoMotor` or `alsoMotorReversed`), rebuild, try again.
Chain or belt on. Run the lift to each named position (low, high...) 3 times.
Pause with gamepad 1 BACK while it moves up: both motors stop at once.
After 2 minutes of use, touch both motors: they should be about as warm as each other.

pass.p: Both motors turn the lifting way (2 of 2) in step 2, the lift reaches each position within its `tolerance` in all runs of step 3, and neither motor is clearly hotter than the other in step 5.

ul: lift or arm, motors (model and gearbox), which method you used (`alsoMotor` or `alsoMotorReversed`)
how the motors face each other (mirror images, or the same way)
any position it missed, and by how much (counts or inches)
the motor temperatures by hand (cool, warm, hot)

different.p: An arm driven from both ends works the same way: test its positions in degrees. If your two motors drive separate slides that are only joined at the top, report how far apart the two sides got (inches), since only the first motor's encoder is read.

tests.title: Odometry Tuner - directions, offsets and the loop check

why.p: Everything that uses the robot's place on the field (driveTo, Pedro paths, odometry aim, shooting on the move) depends on this tuner. It is written for three kinds of odometry. We have tested it on a Pinpoint; OTOS and dead wheels need your help.

ul: The sticks drive at 30% in this tuner. Clear floor, about 6 x 6 ft.
Keep feet away from the wheels while you push or drive.
A robot with an `odometry(...)` line in `Robot.java` ([lesson 7](repo:docs/tutorials/start/07-odometry.md#4-one-line-in-robotjava)).
The small Odometry Tuner file next to `Robot.java`.
A 48 in strip of tape on the floor with a mark at its start, and a tape measure.

ol: Start "Odometry Tuner". D-pad to "Forward 48 in", A. Drive or push the robot 48 in straight along the tape, B. Write what it says.
If it said "counted BACKWARD", add the fix it shows, rebuild, and run step 1 again.
"Left 24 in": A, move the robot 24 in to its left, B. Fix and repeat if it says "counted RIGHT".
"Spin 3+ turns": A, turn in place at least 3 times with the right stick, B. Copy the offsets it shows into your odometry line. Rebuild.
"Loop and back": start on the mark, drive anywhere for about 20 s, come back onto the mark facing the same way, B.
If it shows `Tunables.Odometry: checked = true`, set it in `Tunables.java`.

pass.p: The Forward test is within 2% (48 in counts as 47.0 to 49.0 in), and the Loop test passes: back within 1 in and 2 degrees of the mark.

ul: odometry kind (Pinpoint, OTOS, 2 or 3 dead wheels) and the pod type
Forward test: the % off it showed, before and after fixes
the offsets (or track width) it gave
Loop test: the distance and angle error it showed, and how many tries it took

different.p: A tank robot cannot strafe: push it sideways by hand for the Left test. An OTOS has no offsets to measure (measure `mountIn` with a tape). Dead wheels with the IMU need `.imu(...)` in the drive line. Say which of these you did. Pods in odd places (far off centre, angled) are very useful to report.

tests.title: Set pose here - hold START 1 s on the reset spot

why.p: When TeleOp runs without an autonomous first, the robot does not know where it is. "Set pose here" fixes that with one held button. It must only work when the robot stands still, and never when a driver pairs a gamepad (START + A or START + B).

ul: Real robot: the robot does not move in this test, but keep the sticks let go when you hold START.

A robot with an odometry line, and the reset spot in `Tunables.Odometry` (`resetX`, `resetY`, `resetHeading`, seen from your own drivers' wall). BIOBUZZ: also `mirrorForRed = false`, written once for the whole robot in `Tunables.Aim` (or in `Tunables.Odometry` if you have no `Aim` section).
Simulator: your own robot from `Robot.java` (`./gradlew :sim:fromRobot -PteamCode=../TeamCode`), or the odometry robot from lesson 7.
A tape measure (real robot).

ol: Put the robot on the reset spot (for example the start tile against your wall, facing the field). In the simulator, drag it there on the field map.
INIT your TeleOp (with no autonomous before it). Read INIT's `Set pose: hold G1 START 1 s at ...` line.
Hold gamepad 1's small START button for 1 second, sticks let go. Gamepad 1 buzzes twice and the Driver Station says `Pose set: ...`.
START the TeleOp. Drive about 4 ft away and back to the spot. Read the pose: it should be close to the reset spot.
Push the left stick a little and hold START at the same time: it must say `Pose NOT set: stop first`.
Hold START, then press A (as if pairing a gamepad): the pose must NOT be set.
Choose RED in INIT (X = BLUE, B = RED) and repeat step 3 on the red side: the pose should use the same numbers from the red wall (BIOBUZZ).

pass.p: Step 3 sets the pose within 1 in and 2 degrees of the spot you wrote; steps 5 and 6 do not set it (0 of 2); the RED pose in step 7 matches the reset spot for RED that INIT shows.

ul: the reset spot you used (x, y, heading)
the pose shown after step 3 and after step 4
what steps 5 and 6 showed
the INIT line `Reset spot for RED: ...`

different.p: If you moved "set pose" to another button (`lib.setPose(...)` in `libraryButtons`), use that one and say which. On a field that is a mirror image (not BIOBUZZ), leave `mirrorForRed` out and check that RED mirrors x and the heading. If INIT warns that two places give different `mirrorForRed` values, copy the warning into your report.

tests.title: PathAt - start things along a path while it drives

why.p: `PathAt` starts a part (an intake, a spin-up) at a place along a Pedro path while the robot keeps driving. It is new. We need to know each kind fires once, at the right place, on robots that are not ours, and that the report says when one did not fire.

ul: Real robot: the robot drives a path by itself. Clear floor, PRACTICE profile, hand on STOP.
Use a part that is safe to switch on while driving (an intake, a light). Not a flywheel with pieces in it.
Lesson 8 done: Pedro added, `PedroConstants` tuned, `Tunables.Odometry.checked = true`.
A path with two parts (`PedroPath.line(...).then(PedroPath.curve(...))`), about 4-6 ft long.
Tape marks on the floor where you expect each thing to start (real robot).

ol: Add three things to your `follow` step: `PathAt.fraction(0.5, "Intake on", robot.intake::in)`, `PathAt.part(2, "Intake off", robot.intake::stop)` and `PathAt.inchesLeft(12, ...)` with any part of yours.
Run it in the simulator first: does each start where you expected? (Watch the part, and the Driver Station.)
Run it on the robot (PRACTICE). Watch where the robot is when each one starts. Mark it on the floor.
Measure how far each mark is from where you expected it.
Put a box in the path so the robot stops early (it ends `STALLED` or timed out). Read the report: it should list the things that did not start (`not fired: ...`).
Try a mistake: `PathAt.fraction(2, ...)`. INIT must stop with a message.

pass.p: Each `PathAt` starts once (3 of 3) within 3 in of where you expected on the robot; step 5's report names every thing that did not fire; step 6 stops at INIT with a message that names the mistake.

ul: your path (copy the `PedroPath` line)
for each `PathAt`: expected place, real place, distance off (inches)
the report line from step 5
the INIT message from step 6

different.p: Use any parts you have; a light or a servo is fine. `PathAt.near(x, y, 6, ...)` and `PathAt.inchesDone(...)` are welcome as extra tries. `driveTo` steps take `PathAt` too: if you have no Pedro, try `PathAt.inchesLeft(...)` on a `driveTo` and say so.

tests.title: Hardware Check finds every device and each motor counts up

why.p: The Hardware Check is the first thing every team runs. It must find every device in your robot configuration, on any robot, with no code from you. If it misses a device or shows a wrong hint, every later lesson goes wrong.

ul: Robot on a block: wheels off the ground. A drive motor can spin at 50% power in this test.
Keep fingers out of gears, chains and lifts while a motor runs.
A robot with its configuration made on the Driver Station (any robot: a kit bot is fine).
The 3-line Hardware Check OpMode in TeamCode ([how](repo:docs/tutorials/19-testing-procedures.md#1-the-3-line-opmode)).
A charged battery.

ol: Build and install. On the Driver Station, choose the TeleOp "Hardware Check", INIT, then START.
Count the devices in your configuration. Count the devices the Hardware Check lists (D-pad up and down goes through them).
For each motor: choose it, push gamepad 1's right stick up a little. Watch which way it turns and whether its encoder count goes UP.

For each servo: choose it. Set the start point near where the servo sits (D-pad right and left; nothing moves). Press A: it moves to the start point. Then D-pad right and left: it moves a little each press.
Read the battery line and the IMU line. (The IMU is the turn sensor inside the Control Hub. "Yaw" is the way the robot faces, in degrees.) Turn the robot left by hand: the yaw goes up.
Read each hint the screen shows for a device. Is it right for your robot?

pass.p: Every device in the configuration is in the list (the same count, for example 9 of 9), every motor moves when you push the stick, and the battery line shows a voltage within 0.3 V of a meter (or of the Driver Station's own battery number).

ul: devices in the configuration, devices the Hardware Check listed
any device it did not find (its type in the configuration)
motors whose encoder counted DOWN with positive power
the battery voltage it showed
any hint that was wrong or confusing

different.p: Any robot works: the point is that the check finds every kind of device. Unusual devices are the most useful to report: a second Limelight, an I2C sensor the library does not know (I2C: the small 4-pin ports on the hub, used by colour and distance sensors), or an Expansion Hub (a second hub, joined to the Control Hub by a cable, for more motors and servos). A part marked `optional()` in `Robot.java` that is not in the configuration should show as `optional, so the part is off (fine)`: say if it did not. If a device type is missing from the list, say its type exactly as the configuration names it.

tests.title: A part that is not on the robot yet - optional() and the COMPETITION warning

why.p: Robots are built in steps. With `.optional()`, a part whose device is not in the configuration yet is simply off: INIT goes on, its buttons are off, and actions and autonomous skip it. At an event the same thing could hide a misspelled configuration name, so in the COMPETITION profile it is a loud warning.

ul: Real robot: the other parts move as usual. Clear floor, a hand on STOP.
A part in `Robot.java` you can take out of the configuration (an intake, a servo). Add `.optional()` to its line, for example `intakeDeploy = add(Positioner.servo("intake_deploy").optional());`.
An action or an autonomous step that uses it, and a button that uses it.
Simulator: your robot from `Robot.java` (`:sim:fromRobot`), then add `missing = intake_deploy` (your device's name) as a line in `simulator/robot.properties`.
Real robot: a copy of the configuration on the Driver Station without that device (or with its name changed).

ol: INIT your TeleOp (PRACTICE profile). Read the note: `"intake_deploy" not in the configuration: IntakeDeploy is off (optional part)`. INIT does not stop.
Open the button map (GUIDE): the part's buttons say `- off: IntakeDeploy not on the robot`.
START. Press the part's button: nothing moves, no error.
Run the action (or the autonomous): it goes on, and its report says `skipped IntakeDeploy (not on the robot)`.

Choose the COMPETITION profile (the last line of an autonomous's INIT menu; it is saved on the hub). INIT TeleOp again: the very first line is `!! COMPETITION: "intake_deploy" not in the configuration: IntakeDeploy is OFF ...`, and the button map says `!! OFF`.
Put the device back in the configuration (simulator: delete the `missing` line). INIT: the part works, with no code change.
Take `.optional()` off and remove the device again. INIT must stop and name the device. Put it back. Set the profile back to PRACTICE.

pass.p: INIT goes on with the part off (steps 1 to 4, no error), the COMPETITION warning is the first line of the screen (1 of 1), and without `optional()` a missing device stops INIT (1 of 1).

ul: the part (kind and device name) and simulator or real robot
the INIT lines in PRACTICE and COMPETITION (copy them)
the action's report line from step 4
anything that moved, or an error, while the part was off

different.p: Any part but the drive and the odometry can be optional. A part with several devices (a lift with a switch, a launcher with a feeder): only the first device decides. Try removing a second device too: INIT must stop and name it (half a part is a wiring mistake). Say what you tried.

tests.title: Flywheel Finder - gains that hold the speed

why.p: The Flywheel Finder works out the speed-control numbers (the gains) from one full-power spin. Flywheels differ a lot (motor, gearing, wheel weight). We want to know its gains hold the speed on your flywheel, with no tuning by hand.

ul: Safety glasses. Nobody in front of the launcher. No pieces loaded until step 5.
Robot on a block or held so it cannot move.
`Launcher.flywheel("name", "motor-id")` in `Robot.java` (or any flywheel motor with an encoder cable).
The "Flywheel Finder" OpMode (starter kit).
A charged battery (12.5 V or more).

ol: Start "Flywheel Finder". Choose the flywheel motor.
Let go of A, then hold A: full power until the speed stops rising. Wrong way? Let go, press X (reverse), try again.
Press B: it holds a speed. Use the D-pad to set the speed you shoot at.
Watch the measured speed for 10 seconds. Use RB (more F) or LB (less F) only if it stays above or below.
Feed one piece by hand. Read the recovery time.
Copy the `Tunables.Launcher: kP = ..., kF = ..., nominalVolts = ...` line into `Tunables.java`. Spin up in your TeleOp with LB and read the speed.

pass.p: In step 4 the measured speed stays within 3% of the target, and in step 6 your TeleOp reaches the speed and shows READY within 1.5 s of pressing LB.

ul: flywheel motor (catalog id), gearing, wheel (size, weight if known)
the line it printed (gains and `nominalVolts`)
the speed error in step 4 (RPM), and whether you used RB or LB
recovery time after a piece (seconds)
time to READY in step 6

different.p: Two motors on one flywheel, a geared flywheel or a belt: say how it is built. A catapult or a launcher with no encoder cannot use this test: report "could not run" with what you have.

tests.title: Never feeds a slow flywheel, and gives up after 3 s

why.p: The launcher's two safety rules are the reason teams can trust the fire button: a piece is only fed when the wheel is at speed, and the launcher gives up after 3 s instead of firing late. Different feeders (a CR servo, a servo, a roller) must all follow them.

ul: Safety glasses. Nobody in front of the launcher.
Real robot: a few pieces only, a clear space where shots land.
A launcher with a feeder in `Robot.java` and its gains (SHOT-01).
Simulator: lesson 9's goBILDA bot (`-Probot=sim/robots/starter-bot-gobilda.properties`, "goBILDA Bot TeleOp").

ol: INIT your TeleOp, START. Load 3 pieces.
Without spinning up, tap RB (fire one). The wheel spins up and the piece waits; it is fed only when the speed is READY.
Hold RB: pieces fire one after another, each when the wheel is back at speed. Let go: no more are fed.

Make it unable to reach the speed. Real robot: STOP, power the robot off, unplug the flywheel motor's encoder cable, power on (the speed now reads 0, and the wheel may spin at full power: unload every piece first and watch the feeder instead). Simulator: lower the battery on the page (Robot tab) until the wheel cannot reach READY (if it still reaches READY, say so and skip step 5). INIT, START, tap RB.
After about 3 s the Driver Station says `Launcher gave up: flywheel` and the feeder does not move. Real robot: power off and plug the encoder cable back in.

pass.p: No piece is fed before READY (0 of 3), and in step 5 it gives up within 3.5 s and feeds nothing.

ul: feeder type (CR servo, servo, roller motor) and `feedSec` or `pushSec`
pieces fed per RB tap (should be 1)
time between shots while RB is held (seconds)
what the Driver Station said in step 5

different.p: If your feeder pushes two pieces at once, lower `feedSec` (or `pushSec`) and say what worked. A launcher with extra "ready" checks (`requireReady(...)`) should name them when it gives up: report the words you saw.

tests.title: Shot Tuner - build a shot table with hits and misses

why.p: The Shot Tuner builds the speed-for-each-distance table the way experienced teams do: 3-5 shots per speed, each marked HIT or MISS, and the best hit ratio wins. We want to know a team that has never done it can fill a table that scores, in about an hour.

ul: Safety glasses. Nobody between the robot and the goal. Collect pieces only when the flywheel is off (LB).
SHOT-01 done (gains). A camera that sees the goal, or odometry with `Tunables.Aim.goalX`, `goalY`.
A Shot Tuner file for your robot ([recipe](repo:docs/cookbook.md#how-do-i-build-a-shot-table-speed-for-each-distance)).
10 or more game pieces, a tape measure, a charged battery.

ol: Start the Shot Tuner. Two tables (POLLEN and NECTAR)? Press Y until `> Table`, pick one with D-pad left or right, and load that piece.
Park at your nearest shooting distance. Check the distance line says where it came from (camera or odometry). LB starts the flywheel.
Fire 3-5 (RB). After each, press A = HIT or B = MISS. Change the speed with the D-pad and fire 3-5 again. Try 2-3 speeds.
Press X to save the best. Mark one wrong? Left stick click takes it back first.
Move back 1-2 ft and repeat, until `Points:` says 4 for this table.
Copy the line it shows into `Tunables.Launcher`. Rebuild. In your TeleOp, fire 5 from a distance between two points.

pass.p: The table has 4 or more points, and in step 6 at least 3 of 5 shots score from a distance between two points.

ul: camera or odometry for the distance
your table line(s), copied from the screen
hits out of 5 in step 6, and the distance
total time it took (minutes)
any "sagged" warning, and the battery voltage

different.p: Fewer than 10 pieces? Fire 3 per speed. A robot without a camera can use the odometry for the distance: put the robot in the middle of the field facing away from you before INIT, or set `startSpotIn()`. A hood adds a HOOD choice under Y (see HOOD-03).

tests.title: Speed trim on the D-pad, and last match's trim

why.p: Some days every shot is a bit short. The operator trims all speeds by 1% per D-pad press. The trim must stop at 15%, never ask for more than the motor can do, start at 0 every INIT, and only OFFER last time's trim (never put it back by itself).

ul: Safety glasses if you fire pieces. You can do this test without firing (watch the numbers).
A launcher with speed from the distance (`.speedFromDistance(camera)` or `.speedFromOdometry()`) and a shot table.
Two drivers: the trim is on gamepad 2 (one driver: gamepad 1).

ol: INIT, START. Spin up (LB). Read the launcher's first line: `Speed trim: 0%`.
Press gamepad 2's D-pad up 3 times (each press counts when you let go): `Speed trim: +3%`. The target speed goes up about 3%.
Hold D-pad up: one more step every 0.25 s. Keep holding: it stops at +15% (or says `(motor limit)` first).
Double-tap D-pad down: back to 0%.
Trim to +3%. STOP. INIT again: the trim is 0% and the Driver Station says `Trim last time: +3% (double-tap D-pad up after START to use it)`.
START, double-tap D-pad up: the trim is +3%.

pass.p: Each press changes the target by 1% of the table's speed (within 10 RPM), the trim never passes 15% or the motor's top speed, and after INIT the trim is 0 until you double-tap D-pad up (1 of 1).

ul: the target speed at 0% and at +3% (RPM)
where it stopped in step 3 (+15% or motor limit, and the RPM)
the INIT line in step 5
one driver or two

different.p: With a fixed speed (no table) the D-pad changes `speedRpm` by `stepRpm` instead of trimming: report that it did so, if that is your robot. If you put the trim on other buttons in your own code, say how.

tests.title: Battery compensation - 4 quick shots on a tired battery

why.p: Battery compensation is off by default because it is not yet proven on a real robot. This test is how we find out. It should help the wheel get back to speed after each shot on a low battery. If it makes no difference, or the wheel overshoots, we want to know: then we will change the default.

ul: Safety glasses. Nobody in front of the launcher. A clear space where shots land.
Do not run a battery below 11.0 V on purpose: stop when it reaches about 11.3 V.

SHOT-01 done: `kF` and `nominalVolts` in `Tunables.Launcher`, and `public static boolean batteryCompensation = true;` there to turn it on. (Without `nominalVolts`, INIT says `battery compensation on, nominalVolts not written: assuming 12.8 V`: write yours from the Flywheel Finder.)
A battery at about 11.5 V under no load (run the robot for a while, or use an older battery). A full battery for step 6.
A phone to film the Driver Station screen (the speed numbers), or a second person to write them.
8 pieces.

ol: With the 11.5 V battery: INIT, START, spin up (LB). Wait for READY.
Fire 4 shots as fast as the launcher allows (hold RB). Film the launcher's measured RPM and target.
Write the lowest RPM after each shot, and how long it took to get back to READY.
Set `batteryCompensation = false` in `Tunables.Launcher`, rebuild, and repeat steps 1-3 on the same battery.
Compare: with compensation on, does the wheel come back to speed faster?
Put a full battery in, compensation back on (`true`). Spin up: watch for an overshoot (the speed going more than 3% over the target).

pass.p: With compensation on, the time back to READY after each shot is at least 10% shorter than with it off, and in step 6 the speed never goes more than 3% over the target.

ul: battery voltage at the start of each run (on, off)
for each of the 4 shots, on and off: lowest RPM, time back to READY (seconds)
the biggest overshoot in step 6 (RPM)
your `kF`, `nominalVolts`, flywheel motor

different.p: If your launcher fires slower than the wheel recovers, film single shots instead and say so. If you see no difference, that is a real result: report it (then leaving it off is fine). If the wheel overshoots after a battery swap, turn compensation off and tell us.

tests.title: First spin-up with no flywheel numbers

why.p: A new launcher should work before anyone has run the Flywheel Finder. With `kP` to `kF` and `speedRpm` written as `DEFAULT` in `Tunables.java`, the library starts from numbers worked out from the motor in the parts catalog (kF 11.7, kP 1.17, kI 0.117 and 3600 RPM for a goBILDA 6000 RPM motor). We want to know these starting values spin YOUR wheel to its speed.

ul: Safety glasses. Nobody in front of the launcher. No pieces loaded.
Robot on a block or held so it cannot move.
`Launcher.flywheel("name", "motor-id")` in `Robot.java`, with the real motor's catalog id.

In `Tunables.java`, the launcher's `kP`, `kI`, `kD`, `kF` and `speedRpm` written as `DEFAULT` (`import static com.crossbotics.ftchelper.robot.Starting.*;` at the top). Note your own numbers first, to put them back after.
A charged battery (12.5 V or more).

ol: INIT your TeleOp. Read the note `Launcher: defaults from the catalog (...)` and write it down.
START. Press LB to spin up. Watch the speed on the Driver Station for 10 seconds.
Note how long it takes to show READY, and the speed it settles at.
Spin down. Put your own lines back in `Tunables.java`.

pass.p: INIT shows the defaults note, and in step 2 the speed reaches READY within 3 s and stays within 3% of the target.

ul: flywheel motor (catalog id), gearing, wheel (size, weight if known)
the INIT note (its part, kF, kP, kI and speed)
time to READY (seconds), and the speed it settled at (RPM)
the battery voltage

different.p: A geared flywheel or a belt: the catalog speed is the motor's, so say how it is built. A flywheel with no encoder cable cannot use this test: report "could not run".

tests.title: Drive a kit bot in the simulator

why.p: The simulator is how most teams will try the library first. It must start on Windows, Mac, Linux and Chromebooks, with the laptop setup as written. This is the best first test for any team.

ul: A laptop with Android Studio (it brings Java). The library folder (in your robot project, or cloned on its own).
The [laptop setup](repo:docs/guides/simulator.md#laptop-setup-once) done once.

ol: In a terminal in the `ftc-helper-lib` folder, run `./gradlew :sim:run -Probot=sim/robots/starter-bot-gobilda.properties` (or the REV, AndyMark or Studica file). Windows: `gradlew.bat`.
Open http://localhost:8780.
Choose the kit bot's TeleOp (for example "goBILDA Bot TeleOp"), INIT, START.
Set gamepad 1 to "Keyboard". Drive with W A S D and the arrows for a minute.
Try a real controller if you have one (choose it in the list, press a button once).
Run the intake and (goBILDA) spin up with LB and fire with RB.

pass.p: The page opens within 5 minutes of the first command (after the first download), the robot drives with the keyboard, and nothing shows an error in red.

ul: computer and operating system, browser
which kit bot
how long the first `./gradlew` took (minutes)
any step in the laptop setup that did not work as written, and what fixed it
controller tried (and whether it worked)

different.p: This test uses a kit bot file, so your robot does not matter. If you build one of the kit bots, say whether the simulator's robot behaves like yours (speed, size, which button does what).

tests.title: Your own robot in the simulator, from Robot.java

why.p: `:sim:fromRobot` writes a simulator robot file from your own `Robot.java`. Robots are all different, so this is where we learn which parts the simulator gets wrong or cannot draw.

ul: Your robot in five files in your TeamCode, with the library in the robot project.
SIM-01 works on this laptop.

ol: In the `ftc-helper-lib` folder: `./gradlew :sim:fromRobot -PteamCode=../TeamCode`.
Open `simulator/robot.properties` in your robot project. Read the `TODO` lines; fill in the robot's size if you know it.
`./gradlew :sim:run -PteamCode=../TeamCode`, open http://localhost:8780.
INIT your TeleOp, read the button map, START, drive, and use every part.
Run your autonomous. Read the report at the end.
Draw your parts with `looks(...)` shapes ([how](repo:docs/tutorials/start/01-robot-in-five-files.md#draw-your-robot-from-robotjava)) if you want pieces to be picked up and shot.

pass.p: `:sim:fromRobot` finishes with no error, and every part in `Robot.java` (all of them, for example 6 of 6) shows in the simulator's Motors or Servos panel and responds to its button.

ul: your parts (the `add(...)` lines, or a list)
any part that did not show or did not move
errors from `:sim:fromRobot` (copy them)
what was hard in step 2 or step 6

different.p: That is the point of this test: describe what is unusual (a part the library has no module for, a custom `Module`, odd device names). Things the simulator cannot do are listed in the [simulator guide](repo:docs/guides/simulator.md#not-simulated): say if you hit one.

tests.title: Build an autonomous in the simulator with the auto builder

why.p: The auto builder draws an autonomous on the field, runs it with your real robot code, shows where the robot left the plan, and writes the Java and a scenario file. It must read any team's robot and give Java that builds the first time.

ul: SIM-01 works on this laptop.
Your robot from `Robot.java` (`./gradlew :sim:fromRobot -PteamCode=../TeamCode`, then `./gradlew :sim:run -PteamCode=../TeamCode`), or a kit bot's robot file.
A robot project where you can add one autonomous file.

ol: Open http://localhost:8780 and press **Auto builder** over the 3D view. Check the Robot class it picked ("Best fit"), the drive, and **TeleOp next** (your robot's TeleOp).
Pick RED or BLUE. Pick a start spot from the list. Press **Write it for me** for the note.
Simple steps: add a drive, a turn, an action from your `Actions.java` and "park from here". Fix every warning the checks show.
Press **Run**. Watch the purple plan robot and your robot. Read the result table: each step's word (done, STALLED...) and how far off the plan it ended.
If it offers a fix with **Apply** (a 0.3 s wait before a turn), apply it and Run again.
**Copy the Java**. Paste it into a new file in your TeamCode. Build it.
**Save the scenario** and run it: `./gradlew :sim:scenario -Pfile=...` (each line prints ok or FAIL).

pass.p: The copied Java builds the first time (0 errors), every step ends `done` in the run, and the saved scenario passes (every line ok).

ul: the robot (your own or a kit bot) and its drive
whether "Best fit" and "TeleOp next" were right
the result table after the last run (copy it)
any build error in step 6, and any FAIL in step 7
what was hard to find on the page

different.p: A mecanum robot with odometry can also try the **Pedro path** mode (needs a `follower(...)` line for "follow"). A tank robot cannot strafe: the checks should say so. The saved scenario's `expect step N done` lines need the v0.17.0 simulator or newer.

tests.title: Record a test in the simulator, break it, update it

why.p: The simulator's recorder writes a test from what a driver does on the page. We need to know if students can record a test of their own robot, if the suggested checks make sense, and if a recorded test passes when it is run again (a test that fails for no reason is worse than none).

ul: Your robot project with the simulator running your code: `./gradlew :sim:run -PteamCode=../TeamCode`.
Your robot drives in the simulator, and has an autonomous.

ol: Follow [start lesson 10](repo:docs/tutorials/start/10-test-your-robot-code.md), section 2: record a test of your autonomous (INIT, choose the alliance, START, wait for its end, Stop recording).
Read the suggested checks. Write down any check that looks wrong or missing. Save it.
Press **Run it now**. Then run it 4 more times (**Run it again**).
Record a TeleOp test: drive forward 2 seconds, turn, let go, Stop recording, Save, Run it now (5 times).
Change one number on purpose (for example `Tunables.Drive.maxPower` to 0.6), restart the simulator, and run both tests.
For a test that fails: **The change was on purpose: update the test**, **Save the update**, **Run it again**.
Run all tests with one command: `./gradlew :sim:scenario` (from the `ftc-helper-lib` folder).
Put the number back.

pass.p: Each recorded test passes 5 runs out of 5 before the change, the change makes at least one fail, and after the update it passes again.

ul: robot (drive kind, parts), OpMode names
how many of the 5 runs passed, for each test, before the change
each suggested check that looked wrong or was missing
which test failed after the change, and the lines the update changed
the result of `./gradlew :sim:scenario`
anything in the window that was hard to understand

different.p: Any robot that runs in the simulator works. No autonomous yet? Record two TeleOp tests (driving, and your intake or main mechanism). What matters: a recorded test passes again and again, and fails only when the robot really changed.

tests.title: Shooting on the move - standing still nothing changes

why.p: Shooting on the move is off by default until it is tested on a real robot. The first check is the safest one: turned on, with the robot standing still, it must change nothing. Then the measured flight time, which every later step needs.

ul: Safety glasses. Nobody between the robot and the goal.
The robot stands still in this test.
Odometry checked (ODO-01), aim working (AIM-01, AIM-02 or AIM-03), a shot table.
A phone that films slow motion (240 frames a second).

ol: With `shootOnMove = false`, fire 5 from a fixed spot. Count hits.
Measure `flightSec`: film a shot from the side in slow motion, count the frames from leaving the launcher to reaching the goal, divide by 240. Do it near and far.
Set `shootOnMove = true`, `flightSec` (and `flightSecPerIn` if far shots fly longer), and `shooterForwardIn`, `shooterLeftIn` (and `cameraForwardIn`, `cameraLeftIn` for a camera on the body).
From the same spot, standing still, fire 5 again. Count hits. The `Aim: moving shot` line should not show while still.
Push the robot sideways by hand (or drive slowly): the `Aim: moving shot: lead ... deg, ... in` line appears.

pass.p: Standing still, the hits with it on are within 1 of the hits with it off (out of 5), and the lead shown in step 5 is in the direction opposite to the motion.

ul: hits out of 5, off and on
flight time near and far (frames and seconds), and the distances
your `flightSec`, `flightSecPerIn`, `shooterForwardIn`, `shooterLeftIn`
the lead line while moving (degrees, inches)

different.p: Works with a turret or with whole-robot aim (no turret): say which. A camera on the turret is taken to sit at the pivot. If your camera is somewhere else, measure `cameraForwardIn`, `cameraLeftIn` and say where it is.

tests.title: Shooting on the move - strafe past the goal and score

why.p: This is the real test: does aiming at the "virtual goal" make shots score while the robot drives? Only real shots can tell. If it does not help, we will say so in the docs.

ul: Safety glasses. Nobody on the field side where shots go, and nobody in the robot's path.
PRACTICE profile, slow speed first. A driver who keeps turning slow while firing.
SOM-01 passed. A clear lane about 6 ft long, parallel to the goal, at a distance you shoot from often.
15 or more pieces. A friend to count hits.

ol: With `shootOnMove = false`, drive slowly sideways along the lane and fire 5 while moving. Count hits.
Set `shootOnMove = true`. Drive the same lane at the same speed, fire 5. Count hits.
Misses on the side the robot drives toward: `flightSec` is too short. On the other side: too long. Change it and repeat step 2.
Drive faster (about twice the speed) and fire 5.
Optional: put the on/off on a button (`g2.a.toggle(robot.aim().movingShotMode())`) and check it switches.

pass.p: At slow speed, at least 2 more hits out of 5 with it on than off, or 4 of 5 with it on.

ul: drive speed (about, in/s: lane length divided by time)
hits out of 5: off slow, on slow, on fast
the `flightSec` you ended with, and how many changes it took
which side the misses went before the fix

different.p: A tank drive cannot strafe: drive past the goal along a curve and say so. A turret robot and a whole-robot-aim robot both count. If driving and turning at once makes shots go wide, say how fast you turned.

tests.title: Turret home switch (touch or magnetic) - homes at START

why.p: A turret's motor encoder counts from where it was at INIT. A home switch tells the turret where it really is: it turns slowly to the switch at START, and sets its angle again every time it passes it, so a slipping belt is fixed during the match. Two kinds of switch work (a touch sensor and a magnetic switch); we have tested the magnetic one.

ul: The turret moves by itself at START (slowly, at `homingPower`). Fingers and wires away from it.
Hard stops at the wire limits. Start with `homingPower = 0.2` and `homingTimeout = 5`.

The switch on the robot and in the configuration: a touch sensor (e.g. REV Touch Sensor) as **REV Touch Sensor**, or a magnetic switch (e.g. REV Magnetic Limit Switch, a magnet on the turret) as a **Digital Device**.
`.homeSwitch("turret_home")` on the turret's line in `Robot.java`, and `homeAngle` in `Tunables.Turret` ([how to find it](repo:docs/guides/turret-setup.md#2-how-does-it-know-its-angle)).
Simulator: the V2 example robot (a magnetic switch at 0 degrees; commands in [ILK-01](repo:testing/tests/ILK-01.md)).

ol: Turn the turret by hand about 30 degrees away from the switch. INIT. Read the lines `Turret : home switch at ... deg: found at START` and `Turret homing : at START it turns ... slowly to find the switch`. Nothing moves in INIT.
START. The turret turns slowly toward the switch (`homing: looking for the switch`) and stops homing when it closes. Following and "aimed" wait until then.
Point the turret with the stick to a mark you know (straight forward). Read the angle on the Driver Station. Measure the real angle.
Turn the turret past the switch and back 5 times. The angle on the Driver Station stays right (the switch sets it again at each pass).
Unplug the switch (power off first), power on, INIT, START: after `homingTimeout` seconds the turret stops and the Driver Station says `homing failed: switch not found`. Plug it back in.
Rename the switch in the configuration (or leave it out): INIT says `NO home switch` and the start angle is used.

pass.p: After homing, the angle on the Driver Station is within 2 degrees of the real angle (step 3) and still within 2 degrees after 5 passes (step 4), and step 5 stops within `homingTimeout` + 1 s (1 of 1).

ul: switch kind (touch or magnetic) and how it is configured
`homeAngle`, `homingPower`, `homingTimeout` you used
the angle error after homing and after 5 passes (degrees)
which way it turned to home, and whether you needed `homeDirection`
what step 5 and step 6 showed

different.p: If homing turns the long way round, set `homeDirection` (+1 = counterclockwise, -1 = clockwise) and say so. A turret that starts ON the switch has nothing to look for: say what the screen showed. A CR servo turret with an encoder on a motor port homes the same way: say which you have.

tests.title: Turret with no switch - start angle and the angle carried to TeleOp

why.p: A motor turret with no home switch only knows its angle if it starts where `startAngle` says. After autonomous it is somewhere else, so TeleOp starts from the angle the last program ended at (for 5 minutes). If any of this goes wrong, every shot goes wide by the same angle.

ul: The turret moves by itself while it follows the goal. Fingers and wires away from it.
Hard stops at the wire limits.
A turret with no `.homeSwitch(...)` line, and `min`, `max` in `Tunables.Turret`.
A mark or a small jig that holds the turret at `startAngle` (0 = straight forward, the default).
An autonomous that turns the turret (it follows the goal, or a step turns it).
Simulator: lesson 9's turret robot ([the commands](repo:docs/tutorials/start/09-shooter-and-camera.md#try-it-in-the-simulator)): "TurretBot Shoot from Start", then "TurretBot TeleOp".

ol: Put the turret on its mark. INIT the autonomous: `Turret : startAngle 0 deg: put the turret there by hand before INIT, or every angle is off`.
Run the autonomous to the end. Write the turret's last angle.
Within 5 minutes, INIT TeleOp: `Turret : ... deg, carried from the last program (... s ago ...)`. The angle matches step 2.
START TeleOp, point the turret straight forward with the stick, and check the angle reads about 0.

Stop. Restart the robot app (or wait more than 5 minutes). Turn the turret 20 degrees by hand. INIT TeleOp: it must say `no angle from a program before: turn it to startAngle 0 deg by hand and INIT again`.
Write `min = 10, max = 170` (a range without 0) and no `startAngle`. INIT: no stop, and a note says it counts from the middle of the range (90). Put your numbers back.

pass.p: The carried angle in step 3 is within 2 degrees of where autonomous ended, step 4 reads within 3 degrees of the real angle, and step 5 shows the "no angle from a program before" line (1 of 1).

ul: motor, gear ratio, `min`, `max`, `startAngle`
autonomous end angle and TeleOp's carried angle
the real angle vs the Driver Station in step 4
the lines shown in steps 5 and 6

different.p: With `keepAngle = false` in `Tunables.Turret`, TeleOp never carries the angle: say if you use it and why. A turret with an absolute encoder (`.analogEncoder(...)`) knows its angle at INIT: check that its `absolute encoder: ... deg` line is right instead of steps 1 and 5.

tests.title: Aim Tuner - find the camera offset from real shots

why.p: A camera that is not exactly on the launcher's line makes every shot go a little to one side. The Aim Tuner finds the offset with real shots. We want to know the steps are clear and the offset works at more than one distance.

ul: Safety glasses for everyone. Nobody in front of the launcher.
Hard stops on the turret (if any).
Flywheel gains found (SHOT-01). A goal you can shoot at, and 10-15 game pieces.
The Aim Tuner OpMode for your robot ([finders guide](repo:docs/guides/finders.md#before-you-start)).

ol: Park the robot 4-6 ft from the goal, facing it. A turret with a home switch: press X first.
Hold A: it aims. Fire with RB.
Shots go left of the middle: D-pad RIGHT. Shots go right: D-pad LEFT. Fire again.
Repeat until shots go in the middle. Write the offset.
Move to a second distance (about 2 ft farther). Fire 5 with the same offset.
Copy the line it prints into `Tunables.java`: `Tunables.Turret: cameraOffset = ...` with a turret, `Tunables.Aim: cameraOffset = ...` for whole-robot aim.

pass.p: At the first distance at least 4 of 5 shots go in after tuning, and at the second distance at least 3 of 5 go in with the same offset.

ul: camera place (on the turret, on the body, how far from the launcher's line)
the offset you ended with (degrees)
hits out of 5 at each distance, and the two distances
how many tries it took

different.p: Without a turret the robot itself turns to aim: hold A the same way. If the offset that works changes with distance, your camera is to the side of the launcher: say how far, and which offset worked where.

tests.title: Choose the start spot in the INIT menu

why.p: One autonomous can start from two spots: a `Start` line in the INIT menu picks the steps AND the start (`start(...)` inside an `onlyIf`). The "Place robot" note, the simulator's robot and the odometry's start follow the choice while the drivers change it. If the note shows the wrong spot, the drive team puts the robot in the wrong place.

ul: Real robot: the autonomous drives by itself. Clear floor, everyone out of its way, a hand on STOP, PRACTICE profile.

An autonomous with a menu line and a `start(...)` for each option, like [example 2](repo:docs/guides/autos.md#example-2-one-opmode-the-drivers-choose-in-init): `s.menuChoice("Start", "Near", "Far")`, then `s.onlyIf("Start", "Near").start("NEAR: ...", ...)...end()` and the same for "Far".
Simulator: your robot from `Robot.java` (`./gradlew :sim:fromRobot -PteamCode=../TeamCode`, then `./gradlew :sim:run -PteamCode=../TeamCode`).

ol: INIT the autonomous. Read `Place robot : NEAR: ...` (the first option is chosen at INIT).
With the D-pad, go down to the `Start` line and change it to Far. The note changes to `FAR: ...` at once. Simulator: the robot on the field map moves to the far spot.
Change it back to Near, then to Far again. The note follows every change.
Put the robot on the far spot. START. Read the report at the end: the far steps ran, the near ones did not.
With odometry: INIT a TeleOp right after and read the `Pose` line: it starts from where the far route ended.
Spell an option differently in `onlyIf` (say "far"). INIT, choose Far: nothing in that block runs. Say whether the screen helped you find it. Put it back.

pass.p: The "Place robot" note matches the chosen option every time it changes (at least 3 changes, 3 of 3), and the run in step 4 starts from the far spot and runs only the far steps.

ul: your two `start(...)` lines and notes
simulator or real robot; with or without odometry
the report lines from step 4
what step 6 showed

different.p: Any drive works. Without odometry the start spot is only the note and the simulator's place: check the note. A `parkWithSeconds(...)` inside an `onlyIf` follows the menu the same way: try it if you use one.

tests.title: Move or free the library's buttons

why.p: Every library button (slow, field-centric, pause, menus) can move to another button or be freed for your own job. INIT must catch two jobs on one button and say which button.

ul: Real robot: low power. Check that SOME button still pauses the robot before you drive.

Your `Controls.java`. Inside its class, just after the closing `}` of the `buttons(...)` method, add `@Override protected void libraryButtons(LibraryButtons lib, Pad g1, Pad g2) { }` (the whole method is in the [buttons guide](repo:docs/guides/buttons.md#moving-the-librarys-buttons)), and `import com.crossbotics.ftchelper.teleop.LibraryButtons;` at the top of the file.

ol: Move one library job your drivers want elsewhere, for example `lib.slow(g1.rt);` or `lib.fieldCentric(g1.x);`.
INIT: read the button map. The job is on its new button; the old one is listed as free.
START and check the job works on the new button and the old one does nothing.
Put one of your own jobs on the same button as a library job. INIT must stop and name the button.
Free the pause: `lib.pause(null);`. INIT must warn that nothing pauses the robot. Put it back.

pass.p: The moved job works on its new button (1 of 1), step 4 stops INIT with the button's name, and step 5 shows the warning.

ul: the lines you wrote in `libraryButtons`
the INIT messages from steps 4 and 5 (copy them)
whether the button map was easy to read

different.p: Move whatever your drivers really want moved: that is the best test. One driver (`oneDriver = true`): library jobs you put on `g2` go on gamepad 1: check that.

tests.title: Switch the alliance during TeleOp (turned on by you)

why.p: If autonomous ran as the wrong alliance, the drivers can switch it in TeleOp, but only if the team turned it on. It takes 1.5 s on purpose, so it never happens by accident. With odometry on BIOBUZZ, the pose cannot be fixed, so the odometry aim must switch off until the pose is set again.

ul: Real robot: the robot does not need to move. Sticks let go.
`lib.switchAlliance(g1.start, g1.back);` in `libraryButtons(...)` in `Controls.java` (START first, then BACK; see [CTL-02](repo:testing/tests/CTL-02.md) for where the method goes).
A camera with `.goal(...)` or odometry aim makes the test better (optional).

ol: INIT. Read the `Switch alliance` line. Choose BLUE (X). START.
On gamepad 1, hold the small START button, then press BACK, and hold both for 1.5 s. Both gamepads buzz twice and the screen says `Alliance now RED (was BLUE)`.
Tap START, then BACK quickly: that is the debug lines, not a switch.
With a camera: the goal it looks for switched to RED's.
With odometry on BIOBUZZ (`mirrorForRed = false`): the note says the odometry aim is OFF until the pose is set. Hold START 1 s on the reset spot: it comes back.
Without the `switchAlliance` line: holding START, then BACK does not switch (the INIT line says it is off).

pass.p: The switch happens only after the full 1.5 s hold (1 of 1), never on a quick press (0 of 3 tries), and never without the `switchAlliance` line (0 of 1).

ul: what the screen said in steps 2 and 5
whether the goal (camera) followed
how many quick presses you tried in step 3

different.p: With no camera and no odometry, steps 4 and 5 do not apply: say so. If you put the switch on other buttons, use those.

tests.title: Follow one main-track lesson from start to end

why.p: Each lesson builds on your own robot, a few lines at a time. We check our lessons on our robots; yours will show where a lesson assumes something about the robot that is not true for you.

ul: Follow the lesson's own safety notes ("Check it on the robot"). Low power for the first runs.
Lessons before it done (the lesson says which).
Pick the lesson your team needs next (1 to 9).

ol: Write the lesson number. Start a timer.
Read the lesson top to bottom once without changing code.
Do it: make each change in your own five files, as the lesson says.
Do its "Try it in the simulator" part, then its "Check it on the robot" part.
Each time you are stuck for more than 2 minutes, write the section and the words.
Stop the timer when its last check passes.

pass.p: Every check in the lesson's "Check it on the robot" (or simulator) part passes (all of them, for example 5 of 5), and the time is within 2 times what the lessons page says.

ul: lesson number, time it took (minutes)
each place you got stuck (section and words)
any code in the lesson that did not build (copy the error)
what your robot has that the lesson robot does not (or the other way round)

different.p: The lessons explain with example robots (the lesson robot, the kit bots, the turret robot). Write what you had to change because your robot is different: that is the most useful part of the report.

tests.title: Start from zero on a new laptop

why.p: "Start from zero" installs Android Studio, gets the robot project and makes a first edit. Laptops differ a lot (school-managed Windows, old Macs, Chromebooks). We need to know where it breaks.

ul: A laptop that has never had Android Studio (a school laptop is the best test).
Internet. About 10 GB free disk.

ol: Start a timer. Follow [Start from zero](repo:docs/start-from-zero.md) from the top, exactly as written.
Write each step that did not match your screen (a button with another name, a missing menu).
Go on until its last section: a first build and an edit that builds.
Then run the simulator once (SIM-01 step 1 to 3).

pass.p: A first build passes within 75 minutes (not counting download time), and the simulator page opens.

ul: laptop, operating system and version, school-managed or not
Android Studio version
time (minutes), and download time if slow
each step that did not match your screen
any blocker (admin rights, firewall, disk space) and what fixed it

different.p: No robot needed. If your school blocks installs, say what was blocked: we can add a note for mentors.

tests.title: Lesson 10 from start to finish - record, break and update a test

why.p: Lesson 10 teaches simulator tests with the new "Record a test" button. Most students never wrote a test before. We need to know if the lesson is clear enough to follow alone, on a robot that is not ours.

ul: Your robot project with the library v0.17.1 or newer, and the simulator working (SIM-01).
No robot needed.

ol: Start a timer. Follow [lesson 10](repo:docs/tutorials/start/10-test-your-robot-code.md) from the top, exactly as written, with your own robot (or its "Try it with goBILDA's starter bot").
Record one TeleOp test and one autonomous test, and save both.
Run each one: both should say `PASSED`.
Change one number in `Tunables.java` that the test should notice (for example a slower drive), build, and run the tests again: at least one should say `FAILED`.
Use "The change was on purpose: update the test", save, and run again: `PASSED`.
Put the number back. Run all your tests with the one command from section 8.
Write each sentence or step that did not match your screen, or that you had to read twice.

pass.p: Both tests pass, fail after the change in step 4, and pass again after the update, within 45 minutes, with no help from outside the lesson.

ul: time (minutes)
which robot (kit or your own)
each step that did not match your screen, and each sentence you had to read twice
which checks the recorder ticked for you, and any you changed
did a test ever fail when you changed nothing (how often)

different.p: Any robot works: the tests check what your robot does. If your robot has no autonomous yet, record two TeleOp tests instead and say so.

tests.title: Field-centric driving and resetting "forward"

why.p: Field-centric driving (stick up = away from the driver, whichever way the robot faces) depends on the IMU or the odometry heading. A wrong hub mounting (`.imu(...)` line) makes it drive the wrong way. We want to know it works on robots built differently from ours.

ul: Clear floor, about 6 x 6 ft. Low power (`practiceMaxPower` 0.4, PRACTICE profile).
A hand near STOP.
A mecanum robot in five files, with the `.imu(...)` line set for how your hub is mounted.
Two drivers: gamepad 1 drives. One driver: the same buttons (see the button table in the buttons guide).

ol: INIT your TeleOp with the robot facing away from you, START.
Press Y on gamepad 1 (one driver: right stick click) to switch field-centric on. The Driver Station says it.
Turn the robot 90 degrees left with the right stick. Push the left stick up: the robot should drive away from you, not to its own front.
Turn the robot to face you. Push the left stick up: it still drives away from you.
Turn the robot 45 degrees. Hold gamepad 1 BACK for 1 second: the robot pauses at the press, and after 1 s "forward" becomes the way it faces now. Let go, then tap BACK to go on.
Push the left stick up: the robot now drives the way it faced when you held BACK.

pass.p: In steps 3 and 4 the robot drives away from the driver within about 10 degrees, and after the reset in step 5 "forward" is within about 10 degrees of the way the robot faced.

ul: how the Control Hub is mounted (logo and USB directions in your `.imu(...)` line)
the angle error you saw in steps 3, 4 and 6 (about, in degrees)
what the Driver Station said when you held BACK

different.p: With odometry, field-centric uses the odometry heading instead of the IMU: say which you have. If you moved field-centric or pause to other buttons (`libraryButtons`), use yours and say which. Tank drives cannot strafe, so this test is for mecanum only.

tests.title: Hood follows the shot table, and the hood trim

why.p: With a hood, each table row has a third number: the hood. The launcher blends it between rows like the speed. The operator's left stick adds a hood trim. INIT must stop on a row outside the hood's stops.

ul: Safety glasses if you fire. The hood moves at START (to `startAngle`).
HOOD-01 or HOOD-02 done. A table with three numbers per row, `{inches, rpm, hood}`.
Speed from distance (camera or odometry).
Simulator: your robot from `Robot.java` (`:sim:fromRobot` writes the hood), or `turretbot` from lesson 9.

ol: INIT, START. Drive to a distance halfway between two rows. Read `Hood: ... (table)`: it should be halfway between the two rows' hood numbers.
Gamepad 2 left stick up for a moment: `Hood: ... (table, trim +...)`.
Double-tap D-pad down: both trims (speed and hood) go back to 0.
Shot Tuner: Y until `> Hood`, change the hood with the D-pad, fire, mark HIT/MISS, X saves the speed and hood together.
Put a row with a hood number past a stop in `Tunables.java`. INIT: it must stop with a message naming the row.

pass.p: In step 1 the hood is within 1 degree (or 0.01 servo position) of halfway, step 3 clears both trims, and step 5 stops INIT (1 of 1) with the row's distance in the message.

ul: the two rows and the hood value shown in step 1
the trim step size you saw (degrees per moment of stick)
the INIT message in step 5
in the simulator: did the shot angle change with the hood?

different.p: Without `angleA`, `angleB` the hood works in servo positions (or ticks): the table's third number is a position then. Say which you use. A linkage with a `calibration` table is a good extra test.

tests.title: Hood at START, and the stick with no goal in view

why.p: At START the hood goes to its `startAngle`. While the shot table sets the angle, the operator's stick is a small trim; while no goal is seen (no distance yet), the same stick moves the hood itself, so the operator always sees the stick do something. A hood can also be part of an interlock rule. We want to know this is clear to drivers on robots with a servo hood and with a motor hood.

ul: The hood moves at START. Fingers away from it. Flywheel off for steps 1 to 4.
Hard stops at both ends (`posA`, `posB` measured with the Hood Finder: HOOD-01 or HOOD-02).
A hood with its `Tunables.Hood` numbers (`posA`, `posB`, optional `angleA`, `angleB`) and `startAngle`.
A shot table with a hood column (`{inches, rpm, hood}`) and speed from the distance.
Simulator: the V2 example robot (a servo hood, commands in [ILK-01](repo:testing/tests/ILK-01.md)), or your robot from `Robot.java`.

ol: INIT: the hood does not move, and the launcher's hood line says it goes to its start angle at START.
START: the hood goes to `startAngle`. Read the hood's line (named after its device, e.g. `Hood : 0.0 deg (by hand)`, or `(table)` once a goal is seen).
With the goal out of view (camera covered, or the robot turned away): push gamepad 2 left stick up for 1 s. The hood itself moves (the angle changes, `by hand`), and stops at its stop.
Turn to the goal: the table takes over (`(table)`), and the same stick now adds a trim (`table, trim +...`).
Double-tap gamepad 2 D-pad down: the trim goes back to 0.

In your code, if you use the hood's methods: `angle()` is where it is now, `targetAngle()` where it is going, `isAtTarget()` whether it is there, `goToStart()` sends it to `startAngle`. Build: the old names (`home()`, `homeAngle`, `isArrived()`) must not be used anywhere.

pass.p: At START the hood ends within 1 degree (or 0.01 servo position) of `startAngle` (1 of 1), in step 3 the stick moves the hood with no goal in view (1 of 1), and in step 4 the table sets it again.

ul: servo or motor hood, and its range (degrees or positions)
`startAngle`, and where the hood really ended at START
the hood lines in steps 2, 3 and 4 (copy them)
whether the drivers understood "by hand" vs "table"

different.p: A hood with no `angleA`, `angleB` works in servo positions (or ticks): the numbers on the screen are positions then.
