If your hood and another part can hit, put it in an interlock rule (for example `keepApart("HoodTurret", launcher.hood().zone(), turret.zone());` in `Robot.java`, see the [interlocks guide](repo:docs/guides/interlocks.md)) and also run [ILK-01](repo:testing/tests/ILK-01.md).

tests.title: The alliance on the light at INIT

why.p: A wrong alliance pick in INIT makes the robot aim at the other alliance's goal all match. The drive team sees the light from the field, not the Driver Station's small text, so before START the light shows the alliance. We want to know it is easy to read on real lights, from the drive team's place.

ul: Nothing moves in this test until step 5. Then the usual: a clear floor and a hand on STOP.
A light in `Robot.java` (`Lights.gobilda("light")` or `Lights.blinkin("blinkin")`), with no `allianceAtInit` line in its Tunables section.
Your own rules in `Controls.java` (any, for example lesson 9 section 13's).
Simulator: the light is a dot on the robot (V2 example robot, or your own robot from `Robot.java`).

ol: Restart the robot app (so no alliance is remembered). INIT your TeleOp. Before you pick: the light blinks white once a second.
Press X on gamepad 1 (BLUE): solid blue. Press B (RED): solid red.
Stand where the drive team stands (about 6 ft away, from the side of the robot). Can you tell red from blue? From the front and the back?
START: a 1 s flash of the alliance, then your rules.
Run an autonomous on RED to its end, then INIT TeleOp: the light is red at once (TeleOp took the alliance from autonomous).
Write `public static boolean allianceAtInit = false;` in the light's Tunables section (named after its device, e.g. `Tunables.Light`). INIT: now your rules show in INIT, and no flash at START.

pass.p: Each state shows the right colour (4 of 4: blinking white, blue, red, the flash at START), and two people can tell red from blue from 6 ft away.

ul: light model, and where it sits on the robot
whether red and blue were easy to tell apart, and from where
any colour that looked wrong (and which `allianceColors(...)` fixed it, if you tried)
what step 6 showed

different.p: If your light shows red or blue badly, try `robot.lights.allianceColors(LightColor.PURPLE, LightColor.ORANGE);` in `Controls.java` (blue's colour first) and say whether it is better. A REV Blinkin with a strip of your own: say the strip and its length.

tests.title: A servo's full range - 300 degrees instead of 270

why.p: The hub sends a servo a pulse from 600 to 2400 microseconds for positions 0 to 1. Most FTC servos take 500 to 2500, so part of their turn is never used: a goBILDA 2000 servo turns 270 of its 300 degrees. `.fullRange()` sends the whole range. The numbers come from the sellers' pages; we want them checked on real servos.

ul: Take the servo off its part (or free its linkage) for steps 1 to 4: at full range it turns further and can push on a stop.
Listen for a humming servo: a servo pushing on something. Back off at once.
A servo on a REV hub (Control Hub, Expansion Hub or Servo Hub) with a horn and a mark on it.
The Servo Finder OpMode, and a phone angle app or a printed protractor.
The seller's range for your servo (goBILDA 2000: 300 degrees over 500-2500 us; REV Smart Robot Servo: 270; Axon MK2: up to 360).

ol: Start the Servo Finder. Choose the servo (do NOT press Y). Go to 0, measure the angle. Go to 1, measure. Write the difference.
Stop. Start it again and press **Y** while choosing the servo (full range). Go to 0 and to 1 again. Measure.
Compare both with the [table](repo:docs/modules/hardware.md#full-range): normal range about 90% of the seller's, full range about all of it.

Put the servo back on its part. Add `.fullRange()` to the part's line in `Robot.java` (for example `Claw.servo("claw").fullRange()`). Measure its positions again with the Servo Finder (Y on) and copy the new numbers into `Tunables.java`.
INIT your TeleOp: no note that the servo cannot change its pulse. Run the part to each position.

pass.p: The normal range and the full range are each within 5 degrees of the table's numbers for your servo (2 of 2), and with `.fullRange()` the part reaches every position it was measured at (all of them).

ul: servo model and the hub it is on
the angle from 0 to 1: normal range, full range
the positions before and after (they change with the range)
any INIT note about the pulse range

different.p: A servo on something other than a REV hub cannot change its range: INIT says so and nothing changes; report that. An Axon or REV servo programmed to a smaller range turns less: say how it was programmed. A servo turret or hood has `.fullRange()` too ([TUR-03](repo:testing/tests/TUR-03.md), [HOOD-01](repo:testing/tests/HOOD-01.md)).

tests.title: driveTo a field point - how close does it stop?

why.p: `driveTo` drives straight to a field point while it turns. How close it stops depends on your drive numbers and your odometry. We want real numbers from many robots, not only ours.

ul: PRACTICE profile and `Tunables.Drive.practiceMaxPower` 0.4 for the first runs.
The robot drives by itself: a clear path, everyone out of it, a hand on STOP.
ODO-01 passed (`Tunables.Odometry.checked = true`).
An autonomous with one `driveTo` step, for example lesson 7's "To the Goal" (start at -56, -61; drive to -30, -30 facing 45).
Tape on the floor at the start spot and at the target point.

ol: Put the robot exactly on the start spot. INIT the autonomous, check for the odometry "ready" line.
START. Let it drive to the point and stop.
Measure the robot's centre against the target point (x and y error), and its heading error.
Do it 3 times. Write each.
Run it once more and gently push the robot sideways during the drive: it should come back on course.
Read the report at the end of autonomous.

pass.p: Each of the 3 runs ends within 1.5 in of the point and 3 degrees of the heading, and the push in step 5 does not stop it from arriving.

ul: start spot and target point you used
the 3 errors (x, y in inches; heading in degrees)
the report line for the `driveTo` step (done, STALLED, TIMED_OUT...)
the drive numbers you changed (`turnKp`, `moveMinPower`...), if any

different.p: Use any start spot and point that fit your space; about 3-4 ft of driving is enough. A heavy robot or a robot with small wheels may need `moveMinPower`: say what you changed. Tank robots cannot use `driveTo` (INIT stops with a message): report "could not run" only if that message was unclear.

tests.title: TeleOp starts where autonomous ended

why.p: The pose (where the robot is and which way it faces) should carry from autonomous into TeleOp, so field-centric driving and the odometry aim are right from the first second of TeleOp.

ul: Real robot: the autonomous drives by itself. Clear floor, hand on STOP, PRACTICE profile.
A robot with odometry and any autonomous that drives and ends somewhere you can measure.
Simulator: lesson 7's commands (`odometrybot`, "Odometry Bot To the Goal", then "Odometry Bot TeleOp"), or your own robot.

ol: Run your autonomous to the end.
Within 5 minutes, INIT your TeleOp. Read the `Pose` line.
Compare it with where the robot really is (tape measure, or the simulator's line under the field map).
START and push the left stick up with field-centric on: the robot drives away from the driver.
Wait more than 5 minutes after an autonomous, then INIT TeleOp again: the pose should NOT carry over.

pass.p: The TeleOp pose in step 2 is within 1 in and 2 degrees of where the autonomous ended, and after 5 minutes (step 5) it does not carry over (1 of 1).

ul: the autonomous's end pose and TeleOp's first pose
what TeleOp showed in step 5
the odometry kind

different.p: Any autonomous works, as long as it ends with the robot standing still. One rule for field numbers: your code (and the Driver Station's `Pose` line) uses the field seen from **your own** drivers' wall. Only the simulator's field map line and scenario checks use the field seen from the red wall, so on BLUE their signs flip and the heading differs by 180.

tests.title: The Pedro example path in the simulator

why.p: Lesson 8 says "try it in the simulator first". This checks that the commands and what the lesson says you will see are right on your laptop. No robot needed.

ul: A laptop with the library and the simulator set up ([laptop setup](repo:docs/guides/simulator.md#laptop-setup-once)).
A terminal in the `ftc-helper-lib` folder.

ol: Run `./gradlew :sim:fromRobot -PteamCode=none -ProbotClass=com.crossbotics.ftchelper.examples.pedrobot.Robot -Pout=build/pedrobot.properties`.
Run `./gradlew :sim:run -PteamCode=none -Probot=build/pedrobot.properties` and open http://localhost:8780.
Choose "Pedro Bot Curve to the Goal", choose RED in the INIT menu, INIT, START.
Watch: a short line, then a curve to the goal without stopping, turning to 45 degrees. The intake starts about halfway.
Look at the field map (Control Hub, Robot tab): the orange dashed plan and the green trail.
Read the report at the end.

pass.p: The report says `done` for every step (all of them, for example 5 of 5), the green trail stays within about 2 in of the orange plan, and the intake starts within about 6 in of halfway.

ul: your computer (Windows, Mac, Linux, Chromebook) and browser
the report lines
how long the two Gradle commands took the first time (minutes)
anything on screen that did not match lesson 8

different.p: This test uses the library's example robot, so your robot does not matter. If you have Pedro in your own project, also try your own autonomous (lesson 8 section 6, "Your own robot") and say so.

tests.title: Path Builder web page - draw a path, copy the code, run it

why.p: The Pedro Path Builder (https://crossbotics.com/ftc-helper/path-builder/) draws the BIOBUZZ field, shows where the robot would hit things, and writes the `PedroPath` code. We want to know the code it writes drives the same path in the simulator, and that the page is easy to use.

ul: A browser (a laptop is best; also try a phone if you can).
For step 5: the Pedro example robot in the simulator (see PATH-01).

ol: Open the Path Builder. Make a path with a line and a curve that goes around a field element.
Drag the points until the page shows no red (no hits).
Copy the code it writes.

Paste it into the Pedro example autonomous (`examples/.../pedrobot/autos/CurveToTheGoal.java`, the `TO_GOAL` line) in your library folder (put the old line back afterwards), or into your own autonomous.
Run it in the simulator (PATH-01's commands). Compare the orange plan on the simulator's map with the drawing in the Path Builder.

pass.p: The code builds the first time, and the simulator's orange plan matches the Path Builder's drawing within about 2 in at every point; no hit in the simulator where the builder showed none.

ul: browser and device
the code you copied
any place where the simulator and the builder disagreed (where, how much)
what was hard to do on the page

different.p: Your robot's size matters for hits: if the builder lets you set the robot size, use yours. A robot bigger than 18 x 18 in that hits in the simulator but not in the builder is a good report.

tests.title: Piece Tuner - can the sensor tell the pieces apart?

why.p: A colour sensor (or a distance sensor) tells the robot which piece it holds: POLLEN or NECTAR, red or blue. How well it works depends on where the sensor is mounted and the light. We want readings from many mounts.

ul: Nothing moves in this test. Keep fingers out of the intake if it is powered.
A `Pieces` or `PieceSensor` line in `Robot.java` ([lesson 9 section 12](repo:docs/tutorials/start/09-shooter-and-camera.md#12-extra-know-which-piece-fires-next)).
The Piece Tuner file for your robot ([recipe](repo:docs/cookbook.md#how-do-i-tune-the-piece-sensors)).
One of each game piece.

ol: Start the Piece Tuner. D-pad up/down chooses the sensor.
Put a POLLEN where it really sits (or passes). D-pad left/right to POLLEN, press A, hold still.
Do the same for each kind (RED_NECTAR, BLUE_NECTAR), then EMPTY with nothing there.
Read any warning (two kinds too close, EMPTY looks like a piece).
Copy the lines into `Tunables.java`, rebuild, run it again.
Hold up each piece 10 times, in slightly different spots: count how often "It sees" names it right.

pass.p: Each kind is named right at least 9 of 10 times, and EMPTY reads NONE at least 9 of 10 times.

ul: sensor (REV Color Sensor V3, REV 2m Distance, a webcam) and how far it is from the piece (mm)
the lines it printed
right out of 10 for each kind and for EMPTY
the warnings it gave

different.p: A distance sensor tells sizes apart, not colours: test POLLEN against NECTAR only. Different light (a gym, a window) changes colour readings: if you can, test in two places and say where.

tests.title: Piece count and the next piece picks the shot table

why.p: `Pieces` counts what comes in and what goes out, and says which piece fires next. With two shot tables, the next piece can pick the table. The count can be wrong in real life (two pieces touching, a bounce): we want to know how often.

ul: Keep fingers out of the intake. Safety glasses if you fire.
PCS-01 done (each kind tuned).
`pieces = add(Pieces.kinds(...).comingIn(...).max(4))` before the launcher line; for the table, `.tableFrom(pieces.nextKind())` on the launcher.
Simulator: sensor lines in your robot file (`color.NAME = at=intake`, see [game pieces](repo:docs/guides/simulator.md#game-pieces)).

ol: INIT, START. Run the intake. Feed 4 pieces in one at a time. Read the count after each.
At 4 the intake should stop taking more (if you used `stopsWhen(robot.pieces::isFull)`).
Read `next`: it should be the first piece that went in (or the one at the ready sensor).
With two tables: load a NECTAR next. The shot table line should switch to NECTAR.
Fire them one by one. The count goes down by 1 each time.
Feed 2 pieces that touch each other. Does it count 2?

pass.p: In 10 single pieces fed, the count is right at least 9 times, and the table follows the next piece (the right table for at least 4 of 5 shots).

ul: sensors and where they are
count right out of 10
what happened with 2 touching pieces
shots where the wrong table was used

different.p: A robot with no ready sensor counts only from the intake: say which sensors you have. A robot that holds fewer pieces: use your `max(...)`.

tests.title: DEFAULT, MEASURE and a part not in the catalog

why.p: A new robot's `Tunables.java` can name every setting from day one: `DEFAULT` for "use the library's default" and `MEASURE` for "a number to find on the robot". A motor or servo the catalog does not have can be described in Robot.java (`Motors.custom`, `Parts.customServo`). We want to know the INIT messages make clear what was used, where it came from and what to do next.

ul: Simulator only: nothing moves on a real robot.
Your robot's five files, or `./gradlew :sim:newRobot` from your configuration (it writes the words).
`import static com.crossbotics.ftchelper.robot.Starting.*;` at the top of `Tunables.java`.

ol: Write `DEFAULT` for a few numbers (a launcher's `kF`, a lift's `kP`, a claw's `travelSec`). `./gradlew :sim:fromRobot`, start the simulator, INIT. Write down each "defaults from ..." note.
Write `MEASURE` for one number (a lift's `max`, or a claw position). INIT: write down the message.
Write `DEFAULT` for a lift's `max`. INIT: write down the message. Put your number back.

In Robot.java, give one part a motor of your own: `Motors.custom("my-motor", 28, 5000)` (or a servo: `Parts.customServo("my-servo", 270, 0.16)`). `:sim:fromRobot` again: find its numbers in the robot file. INIT: write down its note.
Change it to `Motors.unknown("my-motor")` on a lift's `.part(...)`. INIT: write down the note.

pass.p: Step 1 lists each value and where it came from; steps 2 and 3 stop INIT with a message that names the number and what to do (the tool for MEASURE, "a safety number" for step 3); step 4 shows the custom numbers in the robot file and "(custom)" in the note; step 5 says "general defaults" and how to do better.

ul: each message, as shown
anything in a message that was unclear, and what you did next

different.p: No lift or launcher: use the parts you have (any Claw, Wrist, Hood, servo Turret or Indexer reads a `travelSec`-like time).

tests.title: A simulator test stands in for a number not measured yet (set tunable)

why.p: A number written as `MEASURE` in Tunables.java stops INIT until it is measured on the robot. The scenario line `set tunable Section.field VALUE` lets a simulator test run before that. We need to know that it works on your robot's code, that it changes nothing for the next test file, and that a typo gives a message a student understands.

ul: Your robot project with the simulator running your code, and one test of yours in `simulator/scenarios/` (record one first: [start lesson 10](repo:docs/tutorials/start/10-test-your-robot-code.md)).

ol: Pick one number in your Tunables.java (for example a servo position). Write down its value.
Change it to `MEASURE` in Tunables.java. Run your test: `./gradlew :sim:scenario`. INIT stops and names the number.
Add `set tunable Section.field VALUE` before `init` in the test (your section and field, the value you wrote down). Run it again: it passes.
Make a second test file without that line (copy the first, delete the line). Run both with one command: the second one stops at INIT again (the number did not carry over).
Make a typo in the name (for example one letter wrong). Run it: read the message.
Put the number back in Tunables.java and delete the `set tunable` line.

pass.p: 3 runs out of 3: with the line the test passes, the next file without it stops at INIT, and the typo message names the right field ("did you mean ...").

ul: the section and field you used, and its type (a number, or true/false)
the result of each run (passed, or the message)
the typo message, and whether it was clear

different.p: Any robot with a Tunables.java works. No `MEASURE` lines? Step 2 makes one.

tests.title: The simulator runs code with MEASURE numbers (stand-ins in the robot file)

why.p: A number written as `MEASURE` in Tunables.java stops INIT on the robot until it is measured. In the simulator, `:sim:fromRobot` writes a stand-in for it in the robot file, so the code runs before the robot is built. We need to know that the simulator uses the stand-in and says so, that the real number wins once it is written, and that the robot file stays right after each `:sim:fromRobot`.

ul: Your robot project with the simulator running your code (`./gradlew :sim:run`), written in five files.

ol: Pick one number in your Tunables.java (for example a servo position). Write down its value, then change it to `MEASURE`.
Run `./gradlew :sim:fromRobot`. Open `simulator/robot.properties`: find the `tunable.Section.field = ...` line for it.
Start the simulator, choose your TeleOp, INIT. Read the note under the Driver Hub ("... = MEASURE: the simulator uses the stand-in ..."). START: the part goes to the stand-in.
Run one of your tests (`./gradlew :sim:scenario`): the `init` line shows the same note, and the test runs past INIT.
Put your number back in Tunables.java and run `./gradlew :sim:fromRobot` again: the `tunable.` line is gone.

pass.p: 3 runs out of 3: INIT goes on with the note, the part goes to the stand-in, and the line is gone after the number is written.

ul: the section and field, the stand-in value written, and whether it was a sensible value for your part
the note text you saw, and whether it was clear
anything the stand-in made the robot do that looked wrong

different.p: Any robot with a Tunables.java works. No `MEASURE` lines? Step 1 makes one.

tests.title: Shooting on the move in the simulator - strafe and compare

why.p: Before anyone tunes shooting on the move on a real robot (SOM-01, SOM-02), the simulator can show whether the lead goes the right way and how much it helps. Its shots fly with real air and its verdicts (clean, rim, miss) come from the same judge as the turret shot simulator.

ul: SIM-01 works on this laptop.

The V2 example robot (a turret that follows the goal, odometry, a shot table, shooting on the move off). In the `ftc-helper-lib` folder: `./gradlew :sim:fromRobot -PteamCode=none -ProbotClass=com.crossbotics.ftchelper.examples.v2bot.Robot -Pout=build/v2bot.properties`, then `./gradlew :sim:run -PteamCode=none -Probot=build/v2bot.properties`. Open http://localhost:8780.
Or your own turret robot with odometry and a shot table (`:sim:fromRobot -PteamCode=../TeamCode`).

ol: Choose "V2 Bot TeleOp", pick the alliance (gamepad 1 X = BLUE, B = RED), START. Open the Match panel (Control Hub, "Match"): it shows each shot's verdict.

Drive to a spot about 4 ft from your goal where the turret follows it (`following: camera`; lesson 9's [Try it in the simulator](repo:docs/tutorials/start/09-shooter-and-camera.md#try-it-in-the-simulator) says where the tags can be seen). Write the spot (the line under the field map).
Shooting on the move is off. Standing still, fire 4 (hold gamepad 2 RB). Count clean shots.

Load 4 pieces again (drive the intake over pieces on the field, or restart the simulator) and go back to the spot. Strafe slowly past the goal (keyboard A or D, or the left stick) and fire 4 while moving. Count clean shots.

Stop the simulator. In `examples/src/main/java/com/crossbotics/ftchelper/examples/v2bot/Tunables.java`, class `Aim`, change `shootOnMove = false` to `true` and add `public static double flightSec = 0.8;` (your own robot: the same two lines in its `Tunables.Aim`). Start the simulator again (the Setup commands).
Repeat step 3 (standing still: no `Aim: moving shot` line) and step 4 at the same speed. While moving, read `Aim: moving shot: lead ... deg, ... in`. Count clean shots.
Misses on the side the robot drives toward: raise `flightSec`; on the other side: lower it (it changes at once in the tuning menu, GUIDE held 1 s). Repeat the strafe.
Put the example's `Tunables.java` back as it was.

pass.p: Standing still, the clean shots with it on are within 1 of what they were before (out of 4), and while strafing it gives at least 2 more clean shots out of 4 than with it off, or 3 of 4 with it on.

ul: the robot (V2 example or your own) and the alliance
clean shots out of 4: still, strafing off, strafing on (and after changing `flightSec`)
the lead the Driver Station showed while strafing (degrees, inches)
the `flightSec` that worked best in the simulator

different.p: A robot with no turret aims the whole robot instead (`g1.rb.toggle(robot.aimMode())`): the same steps work, say so. The simulator's `flightSec` is a starting point only: measure the real one on the robot (SOM-01 step 2).

tests.title: Test kit - JUnit tests of your Robot.java on the laptop

why.p: The test kit gives your robot in five files pretend motors and servos, so a JUnit test on the laptop can do INIT, START and a loop, and check what each motor was sent. A typo in `Tunables.java` then fails on the laptop in a second, not at INIT on the field. It must work in any team's project with no extra Gradle lines.

ul: Your robot in five files in TeamCode, with the library in the robot project.
TeamCode set up for tests once ([tutorial 13, step 3](repo:docs/tutorials/13-testing.md#3-set-up-teamcode-for-tests-once): the JUnit line and `returnDefaultValues`).
No robot needed: this test runs on the laptop.

ol: Make `TeamCode/src/test/java/org/firstinspires/ftc/teamcode/RobotTest.java`: copy the whole file from the [testing guide](repo:docs/guides/testing.md#test-your-robotjava-with-pretend-devices). Change the lift test to one of your parts and its configuration name.
Run `./gradlew :TeamCode:testDebugUnitTest` from the robot project folder (Windows: `gradlew.bat`). All tests pass.
Misspell a field in `Tunables.java` (say `inPowr` for `inPower`). Run again: `tunablesNamesAreRight` fails and names the field. Fix it.
Change a motor's name in `Robot.java` to one the test does not use. Run again: read the message. Put it back.
Write one test of your own: a command to one part, one loop (`robot.all().update()`), then check the power or position the pretend device was sent.
Time a full run of the tests.

pass.p: The tests run with no extra Gradle lines beyond tutorial 13's (0 added), step 3 fails with the field's name in the message, and the whole run takes under 60 s after the first build.

ul: your parts (kinds) and which one your own test checks
any Gradle line you had to add, and the error that made you add it
the failure message from step 3 and step 4 (copy them)
how long the tests took (seconds)

different.p: Any robot in five files works. The test kit cannot show gravity, time passing (an action's `waitSeconds`) or cameras: use the simulator for those. A robot with odometry can use `PretendPinpoint` to put the robot where the test wants: say if you tried it.

tests.title: Servo turret - two measured points and its start angle

why.p: A turret on a standard servo has no encoder and no PID: the library turns an angle into a servo position from two measured points. A servo cannot say where it is, so at START it is sent to its start angle. A small, cheap turret is common on new teams' robots; we have only tried it in the simulator.

ul: The servo moves at START. Fingers and wires away from it.
Listen for a humming servo at the ends: that is a servo pushing on a stop. Back off at once.
`Turret.servo("turret")` in `Robot.java` (add `.follows(camera)` to test the aim too).

`Tunables.Turret`: `posA`, `angleA`, `posB`, `angleB` from the [Servo Finder](repo:docs/guides/finders.md#servo-finder-ends-and-positions) and a phone angle app, and `travelSec` (time a move from posA to posB).
Optional: `.fullRange()` on the line for the servo's whole turn ([MEC-02](repo:testing/tests/MEC-02.md)). Measure posA and posB after turning it on.

ol: INIT. Nothing moves. Read the turret's INIT lines.
START. The turret goes to its `startAngle` (or the middle of its range if you wrote none).
Turn it with the stick (gamepad 2 right stick X) to 0, then to each end. Measure the real angle each time with the phone app.
Turn it to 4 angles between the ends (by stick, or with `robot.turret.aimAt(degrees)` on a button). Measure each.
With `.follows(camera)`: let it follow the goal. It reads AIMED only after `travelSec` has passed since its last move.

pass.p: At each of the 6 angles in steps 3 and 4 the real angle is within 3 degrees of the Driver Station's, and the servo never hums at an end (0 times).

ul: servo model, gears, and whether you used `.fullRange()`
`posA`, `angleA`, `posB`, `angleB`, `travelSec`
each angle: Driver Station vs measured
how long AIMED took after a move (about)

different.p: A servo turret on a linkage (not straight gears) turns unevenly between the ends: say how far off the middle angles were. A continuous-rotation servo with an encoder is a different kind: `Turret.crServo(...)`, see the [turret setup guide](repo:docs/guides/turret-setup.md#1-what-turns-it).

tests.title: Lights - colour rules and a flash per shot

why.p: A light lets the drivers see the robot's state without looking at the Driver Station. The rules must pick the first true one, and the light must never change faster than 5 times a second (game rule R202 J).

ul: Do not point bright lights at people's eyes or onto the field.
`lights = add(Lights.gobilda("light"));` or `Lights.blinkin("blinkin")` in `Robot.java`.
Rules in `Controls.java`, for example the five lines in lesson 9 section 13.
Simulator: the light is a dot on the robot.

ol: INIT: the light shows the alliance, not your rules (solid red or blue once it is chosen; [LGT-02](repo:testing/tests/LGT-02.md) tests that part). START: a 1 s flash of the alliance, then your rules.
Make each rule true in turn (spin up, aim on, ...) and check the colour.
Make two rules true at once: the one written first wins.
Fire 3 pieces (`fire(3)` or hold RB): 3 white flashes.
Wait for the last 20 s of TeleOp (or use a short match timer): yellow blinking.
Film the blinking with a phone (slow motion): count changes per second.

pass.p: Every colour matches its rule (all of them), 3 shots give 3 flashes, and the light changes at most 10 times a second (5 on and 5 off).

ul: light type (goBILDA RGB, REV Blinkin)
your rules (copy the lines)
any colour that was wrong (which rule, what it showed)
changes per second from the video

different.p: Use your own rules; any true/false works. If a goBILDA colour looks wrong on your light, say which LightColor and what you saw.

tests.title: Slip-ring turret - round and round, always the short way

why.p: A turret with a slip ring (a part that carries the wires through a turning joint) has no wire limits. With `.continuous()` the library drops `min` and `max`, always turns the shortest way, and is never "out of range". Few teams have one, so every report helps.

ul: Check the slip ring by hand first: turn the turret 3 full turns each way with the robot on. No device may drop off.
The turret can now turn without end: fingers, cables and other parts away from it.
`.continuous()` on the turret's line in `Robot.java`, and no `min`/`max` in `Tunables.Turret` (they are ignored; remove them).
A way to know its angle at START: a home switch ([TUR-01](repo:testing/tests/TUR-01.md)), an absolute encoder, or the start mark ([TUR-02](repo:testing/tests/TUR-02.md)).
A goal the camera can see (or odometry aim), to test following.

ol: INIT, START. Read the turret line: angles show from -180 to 180.
Point it at 170 with the stick, then ask for -170 (a button with `robot.turret.aimAt(-170)`, or follow a goal there). It turns 20 degrees through the back, not 340 the other way.
With following on, drive the robot in 3 full circles around the goal. The turret keeps on the goal and never says `goal out of turret range`.
Stop. Check the slip ring's wires and the turret's angle against a mark.

pass.p: Every move in step 2 takes the short way (2 of 2 tries, each way once), and after 3 circles the angle is within 3 degrees of the real one with no device lost (0 drop-outs).

ul: slip ring model, turret motor or servo, gear ratio
how it knows its angle (switch, absolute encoder, start mark)
the angle error after 3 circles (degrees)
any device that dropped out (the Driver Station or the hub's lights)

different.p: A CR servo turret with an absolute encoder on a slip ring is a common build: say which you have. If your turret can turn more than one turn but not forever, do not use `.continuous()`: write `min` and `max` (for example -190 to 190) instead, and test that with [TUR-02](repo:testing/tests/TUR-02.md).
